1a:
**Grading note for 1a (deepcopy decouples the serialization of `result[DATA]` from `reply.result[DATA]`)**

Grade this item on substance, not wording: the rubric is pointing at the aliasing relationship between `result` and `reply.result`, so award the point to any answer that conveys, in any logically equivalent form, that because of the `deepcopy` the serialization performed on `result[DATA]` does not show up in `reply.result[DATA]`. It does not matter whether the answer frames this as a counterfactual ("without the deepcopy, the serialization would propagate into `reply.result[DATA]`" — the technically accurate inverse of the literal rubric phrasing is fully acceptable) or as a positive statement ("`deepcopy` makes `result` an independent copy, so serializing `result[DATA]` leaves the reply object untouched"). Exact names are not required: a general but on-point explanation that the mutation performed on the copied result — i.e. the data-serialization step in this code — does not propagate back to the reply object earns the point even if it speaks of "the data field", "the reply", or "the original dict". The relationship also counts when it is unambiguously implied rather than stated outright: an answer saying the ledger stores the serialized DATA while the graph/reply still holds the unserialized DATA has conveyed the decoupling, so no deduction is taken.

Deduct the point only when neither an explicit nor an implied statement of this decoupling appears anywhere in the answer — that is, the answer never connects the `deepcopy` to whether the `result[DATA]` serialization appears in `reply.result[DATA]` — or when the answer's bottom-line verdict denies that the deepcopy matters for the `result[DATA]` assignment, e.g. it concludes the copy is only needed for certain transaction types and that modifying `result[DATA]` is "intentional and safe", since that asserts the opposite of the required fact instead of stating it.
1b:
**Sub-item 1b (−2 points if the answer discusses implications on transaction types other than SCHEMA or ISSUER_KEY):**

Deduct the 2 points only when the answer makes some claim about the behavior of a transaction type other than SCHEMA or ISSUER_KEY — i.e., it says what happens, or does not happen, to that type as a consequence of the code. This includes contrastive or exclusionary framings: if the answer raises other types only to rule them out ("for NYM or ATTRIB the data is not serialized, so nothing changes," "this only matters for SCHEMA/ISSUER_KEY, other transactions are unaffected"), that is still a statement about implications for those types and the deduction applies. It also applies when the answer frames the deepcopy as transaction-type-gated and therefore buggy or risky for the other branch — e.g., claiming that because the copy happens inside the SCHEMA/ISSUER_KEY path, some other transaction type suffers aliasing or loses protection.

Do not deduct when other transaction types appear only as a bare mention or enumeration with no claim attached about their behavior — for example, listing the transaction types the handler can receive, or quoting the conditional that tests for SCHEMA/ISSUER_KEY, without saying what results for those other types. Likewise, do not deduct when the explanation stays type-agnostic and operates purely at the level of object references — that `result` and `reply.result` are the same dict object, so mutating one is visible through the other — and never conditions the risk or the consequence on which transaction type is being processed.
2a:
**Sub-item 2a — "data serialization will be reflected in the ledger" (1 point deduction if not mentioned)**

Award no deduction whenever the answer, anywhere in its response, raises the ledger as a place where the serialized form of the data shows up. The mention must name the ledger specifically — "the ledger," or an exact ledger mechanism such as the ledger append, the txn log, or the merkle tree — as the destination that receives the serialized data. Beyond naming the ledger, nothing further is required: the answer does not have to explain *why* this happens, does not have to tie the outcome to the `deepcopy` call, and does not have to discuss the ordering of serialization relative to the ledger append. Correctness and confidence are likewise not required — an imprecise, hedged, or partially wrong description still counts as "mentioned," since this item asks only whether the topic is discussed. So long as the ledger is raised as a consumer of the serialized data in some form, do not deduct.

Deduct the point if the ledger is never named in this role. Generic statements that the serialized data is "saved," "persisted," "written to storage," "stored in the database," or "sent downstream" do not satisfy the item and get the deduction, even if the intended referent is plausibly the ledger; the answer must actually identify the ledger or an exact ledger mechanism. Also deduct if the answer never connects the serialized data to any such destination at all.
2b:
**Sub-item 2b — "data serialization will not be reflected in the graph" (1 point deduction if not mentioned)**

Award no deduction whenever the answer addresses, anywhere in its explanation, what the graph store receives with respect to the serialized data — and the graph must be named as such. The destination has to be identified specifically as the graph: "the graph," "graph storage," "the OrientDB graph," "`storeTxnInGraph`," or equivalent. An answer that only says the unserialized copy goes to "other consumers," "the client/the reply," "the in-memory copy," or "downstream code," without naming the graph, does not satisfy this sub-item and gets the deduction.

Given that the graph is named, the bar for what is said about it is low in two respects. First, a bare mention is enough: the deduction trigger is "if this is not mentioned," so a single clause such as "so the graph stores the unserialized data" fully satisfies the item; no extended discussion of the consequence is required. Second, the claim need not be stated in the exact negative form. It is enough that the answer states something from which the fact follows — e.g. "the deepcopy keeps the original `result` intact so the graph gets the unmodified dict," or "`reply.result` still holds the dict form when it is stored in the graph." Deduct only when neither the explicit statement nor a direct implication of it is present.

Correctness of the claim is not what this sub-item tests. If the answer explicitly addresses what the graph receives with respect to the data serialization but gets the direction wrong — e.g. asserts that the graph also stores the serialized data — still do not deduct here; the item only requires that the graph's handling of the serialized data be discussed.

Deduct the 1 point only if the graph's relationship to the serialized data is never addressed at all, or if the only thing said about the unserialized copy is attached to some unnamed non-graph consumer.
